title: No Frames, Just Frequencies: Bandwidth-Efficient Deployment-Time Adaptation for Smart Glasses

problem.summary: 1 Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints.
statements: 1 Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints.
We present No Frames, Just Frequencies, a bandwidth-efficient source-assisted adaptation framework that characterizes distribution shifts using compact frequency descriptors computed on-device.
Rather than transmitting camera frames, the glasses compute and send frequency descriptors to a host device that contains a replica of the model.

background.summary: Prior work [52] shows that swapping the low-frequency amplitude components between source and target images supports semantic segmentation domain adaptation: the low-frequency amplitude tends to capture the style and domain-specific characteristics, while the phase encodes semantic content [50].

evidence.quote: Prior work [52] shows that swapping the low-frequency amplitude components between source and target images supports semantic segmentation domain adaptation: the low-frequency amplitude tends to capture the style and domain-specific characteristics, while the phase encodes semantic content [50].

In contrast to prior work, which manipulates frequencies for offline adaptation, we use frequency descriptors as a bandwidth-efficient communication primitive between an edge device and a host, and as the input to the corruption classifier that drives the synthesis of the labeled adaptation data.

solution.summary: 4.1 Frequency Descriptors Radially Averaged Power Spectral Density (RAPSD).
solution.approach: 4.1 Frequency Descriptors Radially Averaged Power Spectral Density (RAPSD).
components: The Radially Averaged Power Spectral Density [42] characterizes the global distribution of signal energy across spatial frequencies.

We compute RAPSD by applying a two-dimensional Fast Fourier Transform to the input image and averaging the power spectral density within concentric rings of increasing radius from the zero-frequency (DC) component, normalized by the number of pixels.
This maps the two-dimensional spectrum to a compact one-dimensional vector of length 𝑁 /2 (for an 𝑁 × 𝑁 input), where each index corresponds to a spatial frequency band.

At the native 224 descriptor resolution, the strongest descriptor (DCT) recovers 93.1% of the gain on ConvNeXtV2-Femto (59.34% versus Oracle - CE 60.91%, from a No Adapt accuracy of 37.99%), 93.3% on DeiT-Tiny, and 94.7% on TinyViT-5M.
